phrases.text: Proposition 2 is about California's savings account for hard times: the Rainy Day Fund.
The Legislature put it on the ballot.
It would require the state to save more in the fund, and to keep making extra debt payments for longer.
Each year, the state spends about 250 billion dollars from its General Fund, the account that pays for most public services.
About half goes to schools, community colleges and universities.
About a third goes to health and human services, mostly Medi-Cal.
Most of that money comes from the income tax.
And much of the income tax is paid by high earners, whose incomes include gains from stocks and other investments.
Those gains rise and fall with the stock market and the economy.
So the state's revenue does too.
In good years, revenue can grow quickly.
In a bad recession or a market crash, it can drop by tens of billions of dollars.
Over a few bad years, the losses can add up to half a year's revenue, or more.
But the cost of schools, health care and other services grows steadily, year after year.
A reserve fills that gap.
The state saves money when revenue is high, and spends it when revenue falls short.
That helps the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases and borrowing in the bad years.
The trade-off: money that is saved is not spent on public programs in the good years.
Before 1980, the state's surpluses and reserves varied widely.
From 1980 to 2014, it saved very little.
In 2014, voters approved the rules the state follows today.
Each year, the state must put part of its tax revenue into the Rainy Day Fund, and more when taxes on investment gains are higher than normal.
Once the fund holds 10 percent of General Fund taxes, deposits stop, and that money goes to infrastructure, like highways and housing, instead.
The state must also make extra payments on pension and retiree health debts, until 2030.
Today, the state has about 20 billion dollars in reserves it can use for any program.
Proposition 2 raises the target from 10 to 20 percent of General Fund taxes.
The state would keep saving until the fund reaches it.
In years when the stock market is booming, it would save even more.
It extends the extra debt payments to 2040, and lets that money pay a wider set of debts.
The State Constitution also limits how much tax revenue the state can spend each year.
Today, money put into reserves counts toward that limit when it is saved.
Under Proposition 2, it would count when it is taken out and spent instead.
The Legislative Analyst's Office says reserves would be higher, which would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenue falls.
It says the state might also make more debt payments than it would otherwise.
The arguments that follow are their authors' opinions.
No official agency checked them for accuracy.
Opponents say it weakens the spending limit voters approved in 1978, making the tax rebates that limit can trigger less likely.
They say it adds no new money for schools, health care, or public safety, and the state should keep its old rules.
And they say its backers soon voted to suspend over 5 billion dollars in deposits.
Their argument is signed by leaders of the Assembly Budget Committee, the Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendments Committee, and Reform California.
Supporters say a larger reserve would protect schools, health care, and public safety from cuts in the next downturn.
They say it makes the state save more of a revenue spike instead of spending it, and that the Legislative Analyst's Office recommends saving more.
And they say the rebate rule opponents cite rewards spending over saving.
Their argument is signed by leaders of the California Professional Firefighters, the Assembly Budget Committee, and the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce.
A yes vote means reserves would be higher, and extra debt payments would continue for longer.
A no vote means the current rules would not change.
Every fact here comes from California's official voter guide and the Legislative Analyst's Office, listed on screen.
